[Source](https://x.com/leapxyz/status/2118387847853908115) · 1920×1080, 25fps, 1000 decoded frames/40.0s video · [atlas](dense-a/2118387847853908115-1/index.html)

**Visual coverage:** all 10 consecutive sheets opened, f0–999. Native still f600 supplements the scan. No audio or normal-speed playback review.

**Observed structure and granular changes:**

- f0–44 / 0–1.76s: small centered introducing copy on near-black. Radial metallic ribs emerge from darkness around the center; copy stays approximately fixed while the environment changes.
- f45–79 / 1.80–3.16s: Leap mark/wordmark replaces the introductory word. Bright spokes sweep around the protected center; the mark is the stable anchor.
- f80–118 / 3.20–4.72s: small company attribution appears below. Expanding highlights articulate the metallic world. Brief near-white inversions at f114–115 and f118 punctuate the identity hold.
- f119–168 / 4.76–6.72s: centered trading-app positioning types/builds word by word over a close, ribbed curved surface. Multiple brief white inversions recur around f166–168.
- f169–226 / 6.76–9.04s: performance positioning appears over a circular turbine-like assembly. Apparent rotation and changing specular light carry motion around the fixed reading area.
- f227–271 / 9.08–10.84s: a large, barely lit Solana-like symbol appears behind the centered built-on statement; this reduces scene complexity after the circular assembly.
- f272–346 / 10.88–13.84s: low camera-like sweep along a ribbed landscape/horizon. Network positioning becomes an asset-coverage statement while the horizon remains stable.
- f347–398 / 13.88–15.92s: close-up ribs dominate diagonally; white flashes punctuate entry. An engineering statement builds across the central line.
- f399–446 / 15.96–17.84s: the same material bends into a quieter diagonal. Copy changes to a discipline statement, so the background transformation gives continuity across the editorial change.
- f447–503 / 17.88–20.12s: soft rounded dark form and Wall Street/internet-money phrasing. Minimal surface contrast creates a deliberate lower-intensity pocket.
- f504–589 / 20.16–23.56s: ribbed tunnel returns; asset-category words replace each other in one central slot. Stocks → ETFs → commodities → crypto. White inversions accent the category handoff, rather than adding new objects for every noun.
- f590–642 / 23.60–25.68s: first richly colored product mosaic: diagonal phone/cards in orange, red, blue, and green with dark chrome. Story-related copy overlays the middle. This color reveal is earned by the preceding monochrome material world.
- f643–678 / 25.72–27.12s: mosaic gives way to a single upright phone against blue-black; apparent pullback establishes the full product object.
- f679–737 / 27.16–29.48s: phone disappears into a near-flat dark blue field with tracking copy, then profit/loss wording. Faint vertical guide/plot lines support the financial topic.
- f738–786 / 29.52–31.44s: chart line becomes the focal subject; apparent close framing transitions to a full phone containing the same chart. Content continuity makes the pullback legible.
- f787–811 / 31.48–32.44s: complete chart-on-phone holds, centered on the quiet dark field.
- f812–889 / 32.48–35.56s: fee-planning and token-burn statements occupy a single reading line; words replace in place with blur/softened intermediate states.
- f890–938 / 35.60–37.52s: early-access phrase then starts-now phrase, with a few pale inversion flashes near entry.
- f939–999 / 37.56–39.96s: centered Leap logo/URL holds. Small legal copy appears below later in the hold; its exact wording needs native inspection rather than thumbnail inference.

**Why the visual system works:** The ribbed metallic geometry, protected center, near-black ground, cool light, and restrained white type make one coherent world. Changes in surface scale and highlight direction provide variety without changing the palette every shot. The later colored product mosaic feels like a reveal because it arrives after a long monochrome preparation. The chart-to-phone reframe preserves the same content through scale change.

**Limits and transfer:** This is a brand positioning film, not a granular task demonstration. Borrow the stable reading anchor, progressive reveal of one material world, and content-preserving pullback. Do not copy financial performance language into another product or treat brief flashing inversions as a universal finish. The pixels alone cannot establish whether camera, mesh, or lights moved; reproduce the visible relationship rather than assert a production technique.

**Context and coverage:** Creator calls these snippets from an Ascend sales video; the retrieved attachment is a simultaneous 2×2 composition, not a complete six-second sales narrative. Both consecutive sheets were opened, f0–179; native f95 was inspected. No audio stream is present in this attachment.

- f0–47 / 0–1.57s: top-left has layered email/payment/PDF windows, top-right a document table, bottom-left a payout summary, bottom-right a customer-status list. Pale lavender/gray textured ground supports white UI; green and purple accents carry status/action.
- f48–73 / 1.60–2.43s: lower-left payout summary gives way to a narrow panel with animated fields; top-left windows continue to move in a shallow stack. The surrounding panel structure stays fixed.
- f74–98 / 2.47–3.27s: green status pills populate in top-left; top-right row is selected; bottom-right statuses remain fully presented. Native f95 confirms exact structural hierarchy: email behind payment form behind invoice PDF, selected customer row, payout totals, and varied customer statuses. Same named customer recurs across panels, providing a possible narrative thread inside the montage.
- f99–128 / 3.30–4.27s: purple approve button becomes dominant lower-left. Bottom-right shifts from the detailed status list to sparse small status/step labels on warm ivory. Top-right detail panel opens at the right edge.
- f129–151 / 4.30–5.03s: lower-left action changes to a white pill, then dark confirmation treatment. Top-right rows turn into green processed-like states, while the right-side panel remains visible.
- f152–179 / 5.07–5.97s: dark payout-approved confirmation holds in the lower-left; a long purple lower-edge action/line appears in the top-right detail panel. Multiple result states are held together.

**Transfer:** Layer real work artifacts to make administrative complexity tangible; link repeated entities across steps; use a saturated action color and a separate status color. The snippet proves the value of localized field/action/result changes against a calm container. A complete film should give each consequential action enough attention and hold time; simultaneous tiny panels are a showreel device and make detailed UI reading difficult.

analysisMarkdown:
[Source](https://x.com/XRarchitect/status/2118426646609096710) · 1920×1080, 30fps, 1371 frames/45.7s · [atlas](dense-a/2118426646609096710-1/index.html)

**Context and coverage:** Creator states the film was rendered entirely with Three.js and recommends Frameboy; this is creator-reported tooling, not independently inspected project code. The recovered film is attached to the quoted [World Labs Frameboy launch post](https://x.com/theworldlabs/status/2118424455873741028), rather than a separate native attachment on XRarchitect’s post. Preserve World Labs attribution; XRarchitect’s tooling statement is context about the linked film. All14 consecutive sheets were opened, f0–1370; native f700 was inspected. The creator asks for sound, but audio was not listened to.

- f0–89 / 0–2.97s: macro-like close view of a small off/on switch on a dark physical surface. The switch sits between readable state labels; very dark warm/colored lighting gives way to neutral gray. A moving light/color accent leads the eye before the full device exists in view.
- f90–149 / 3.00–4.97s: cut/reframe to a raised directional-pad detail and small lower counter. Raking light reveals tactile material and rounded corners; the image remains deliberately incomplete.
- f150–225 / 5.00–7.50s: close view of two center buttons and a small World Labs logo. Apparent camera angle becomes more oblique, exposing shallow relief and material thickness.
- f226–279 / 7.53–9.30s: sweep/tilt across the device's screen area introduces a loading display. Diagonal highlight and softened moving edges connect physical close-up to interface.
- f280–303 / 9.33–10.10s: screen loading text/bar is frontal enough to establish a startup state.
- f304–334 / 10.13–11.13s: full handheld-console-like object pulls away, rotates edge-on, reveals its back, then returns to a frontal view. This is the film's large spatial reveal after several partial views.
- f335–389 / 11.17–12.97s: screen brightens by an expanding rounded/circular light region into a pale loading field. The device holds still long enough to present the new state.
- f390–448 / 13.00–14.93s: cut to an isolated small illustrated cartridge suspended on black. It advances downward toward the unseen device; the object is an explicit input rather than decoration.
- f449–494 / 14.97–16.47s: device rises into the composition; cartridge enters the upper slot. Blue environmental light and blue casing arrive together; an illustrated environment fills the screen.
- f495–599 / 16.50–19.97s: full blue device with live environment view holds and subtly reframes. Content within the screen moves while controls and outer frame remain stable.
- f600–714 / 20.00–23.80s: device moves to the right to make room for a small point/grid-like world representation on the left. Native f700 confirms a white path and camera-frustum symbol inside that representation, a real-time-world-model label above, and a matching environment visible on the device. The split explains operation and output in the same shot.
- f715–789 / 23.83–26.30s: left diagram recedes; floating cartridge thumbnails line the top. The device recenters as the next world begins to replace the current one.
- f790–844 / 26.33–28.13s: dark wooded environment replaces bright street scenery; surrounding light and casing become green. Scene content and product surface palette change as one event.
- f845–897 / 28.17–29.90s: purple/pink environment and matching pink casing/background replace the wooded world. Screen imagery remains independently active.
- f898–947 / 29.93–31.57s: warm desert/creature-like scene appears; casing/light transition toward orange. The repeated cartridge/device grammar makes the variation comprehensible.
- f948–1007 / 31.60–33.57s: green woodland returns with lime casing/light. Top cartridge row persists as selection context.
- f1008–1055 / 33.60–35.17s: bright interior world replaces woodland; lime casing moves toward warm yellow. This is another state switch inside a stable object.
- f1056–1143 / 35.20–38.10s: dusk/city world arrives with purple casing. Apparent push-in gradually makes the screen image dominate.
- f1144–1191 / 38.13–39.70s: the device crops away and the world image darkens toward black. This is an intentional release of the tactile frame before identity closure.
- f1192–1270 / 39.73–42.33s: white folded-bird-like mark appears centrally in dark blue light; floating cartridges form a loose peripheral frame. Wordmark begins assembling beside the mark.
- f1271–1370 / 42.37–45.67s: World Labs lockup holds while the peripheral thumbnails remain spatially arranged. Overall image fades down near the final frames.

**Transfer:** Show purposeful partial details before the full product reveal; carry action through a physical input (cartridge) to a changed screen state; stage diagram and live output side by side to explain a concept; make the ambient world respond to the demonstrated state. Macro, rotation, and pullback earn their place because they reveal material, object geometry, or input/output relationship. Depth and controlled defocus suit physical surfaces here; that does not imply oblique blur is suitable for text the viewer must read.

analysisMarkdown:
[Source](https://x.com/runinfrai/status/2112624102016249952) · 1920×1080, 60fps, 2223 frames/37.05s video · [atlas](dense-a/2112624102016249952-1/index.html)

**Coverage:** all23 consecutive sheets opened, f0–2222. Native stills f150,550,710,900,1000,1150,1500,1800 inspected to read the mechanism and information hierarchy. Claims/prices are observations of this source's marketing, not verified product facts or reusable claims.

- f0–64 / 0–1.07s: tiny scattered green pixels organize around a central agent phrase; a highlighted green label expands into a faint framed application/code panel.
- f65–207 / 1.08–3.45s: panel grows to the right; a large sentence builds on the left, with a green marker-like block tracking the emphasized word. Within the panel, consecutive request cards accumulate beside code. Native f150 confirms recurring context across turns, rather than random decorative text.
- f208–274 / 3.47–4.57s: jagged square/pixel wipe advances diagonally from the upper-left, covering the explanatory UI in green and resolving to a white central mark. The wipe vocabulary is visibly digital and brand-specific.
- f275–375 / 4.58–6.25s: green field holds, then scales down through stepped square silhouettes into a small mark on white; RunInfra wordmark resolves beside it. Background → tile → icon is one continuous semantic scale change.
- f376–439 / 6.27–7.32s: a new short instruction builds with a moving green word highlight. Text gives way to a compact dark technical block.
- f440–557 / 7.33–9.28s: compact block expands into a dark mechanism diagram. Five source calls on the left connect toward a selected warm replica on the right. Lines draw to one destination; native f550 confirms a cold first request and subsequent cache-hit requests, making the routing mechanism visually explicit.
- f558–589 / 9.30–9.82s: pixel wipe dissolves dark diagram into a white field; fragments persist briefly while a statistic sentence begins. The transition reuses the opening digital wipe.
- f590–659 / 9.83–10.98s: cache-hit percentage statement types/builds across the center; green highlight expands under the specific value and noun. It then shifts downward as the next layout forms.
- f660–788 / 11.00–13.13s: two-column layout appears: a dark model/status tile left and green square matrix right. Native f710 confirms model identity, a cache statistic, and a repeated square field. Matrix and model selector change together; the lower statement persists as an anchor.
- f789–830 / 13.15–13.83s: dark tile and matrix disassemble upward via green pixel fragments, clearing most of the canvas.
- f831–921 / 13.85–15.35s: optimized-kernel statement builds at left; code types in a dark right panel. A circular model badge and metrics anchor the lower portion. Native f900 confirms a large key phrase, code panel, and smaller speed/cost/cache metrics, establishing a clear hierarchy.
- f922–1043 / 15.37–17.38s: white comparison chart replaces the code panel; line spans distinguish list versus effective input prices for three model rows. Green endpoint squares, highlighted title fragment, and large footer price statement align to the same grid. Native f1000 establishes this is a price comparison, not a time-series graph.
- f1044–1091 / 17.40–18.18s: green arrow/caret is isolated, enlarged, then shrunk into an introducing-line anchor. The punctuation becomes a transition object.
- f1092–1205 / 18.20–20.08s: introducing phrase resolves into the coding-plan offer. Green stepped highlight grows with the phrase and pauses once complete; native f1150 shows the coarse stepped ends and monospace text.
- f1206–1373 / 20.10–22.88s: central green badge transforms in place through supported agent names/icons. The upper qualifier and badge position remain fixed. Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode variants become one compatibility sequence, not separate layouts.
- f1374–1448 / 22.90–24.13s: badge becomes a compatibility-count claim, then the number deconstructs into the next layout's green bar. Reusing the rectangle reduces visual reset cost.
- f1449–1571 / 24.15–26.18s: left-aligned monthly-price offer and two small benefit lines form above a wide green plans button. A large outlined hand pointer arrives and clicks. Native f1500 confirms the CTA hierarchy before the click.
- f1572–1647 / 26.20–27.45s: CTA bar expands into three pricing cards, with the middle plan highlighted. Pointer remains near the active lower control so action and result remain spatially linked.
- f1648–1740 / 27.47–29.00s: pricing cards dissolve to a sparse source-to-infrastructure relationship line. The small central brand/connection element carries the transition.
- f1741–1892 / 29.02–31.53s: a close code-example UI appears; model/language tabs and highlighted campaign labels build around it. Native f1800 confirms model tabs, SDK/language tab row, copy control, and typed request example. This is a concrete integration artifact after the abstract mechanism.
- f1893–1999 / 31.55–33.32s: diagonal green pixel wipe takes over again, holds the mark, and shrinks back into the wordmark on white.
- f2000–2222 / 33.33–37.03s: quiet centered wordmark holds for the last~3.7s. This is substantially calmer than the middle explanation.

**Transfer:** Define a small vocabulary that can carry both story and transition: green emphasis rectangle, pixel wipe, terminal caret, grid. Show the mechanism before presenting the number, then an offer and actual integration artifact. A narrator could connect these if commissioned, but this study cannot judge audio pacing. Camera-like travel is minimal; most energy comes from layout, scale, masks, and semantic object reuse. A GSAP/SVG/DOM implementation is plausible, not creator-verified. Avoid reusing the source's statistics without product evidence.

- f1222–1289 / 40.73–42.97s: lime paired-shape silhouette and engineering panel. These inserts share the same layout and repeatable identity transition; breadth is communicated without rebuilding every scene.

- f1348–1405 / 44.93–46.83s: message builds and holds. Native f1350 identifies campaign expansion and a contract handoff to legal. This creates a reason for the next person to enter the story.
- f1406–1519 / 46.87–50.63s: person leaves laptop to compare/arrange images at the board; the response/progress area remains on the left. Human work changes after delegation while the visual task state persists.
- f1520–1576 / 50.67–52.53s: response completes and yellow identity object moves through the foreground, cueing the cut.
- f1577–1638 / 52.57–54.60s: purple legal-office set, seated person, binders, paper stacks, cartons, lamp; yellow sphere enters and becomes a legal-channel message. A carried yellow agent identity visually connects the prior studio to the new department.
- f1639–1731 / 54.63–57.70s: message gains a reply from the legal person; native f1700 confirms the previous campaign/contract expansion arrives in a legal channel. This is the key narrative payoff of the handoff.
- f1732–1784 / 57.73–59.47s: prior message collapses/clears; a direct review instruction appears. The role changes from receiving context to commissioning work, while the actor remains in the same scene.
- f1785–1911 / 59.50–63.70s: legal teammate checklist builds; native f1800 shows reading, comparing terms, flagging clauses, and drafting a redline. Person writes in a notebook while checklist progresses; the camera slowly widens, giving the completion process space.
- f1912–1922 / 63.73–64.07s: purple identity shape rises into the near foreground, ending the human-scene chain.
- f1923–2006 / 64.10–66.87s: black field, centered serif work-for-you proposition, and the colorful agent shapes reform around it. This resolves the introduced cast and the human benefit in one frame.

**Story and camera transfer:** The clearest relationship is goal → agent work → person returns to meaningful work → downstream teammate receives a concrete consequence. The film connects selected people through specific tasks rather than listing every feature in isolation. Each set reserves a clean reading zone before adding UI. Slow push/pull changes scene scale while strong human silhouette and large cards remain legible. Large colorful agent objects become small interface identities; later the same identities carry messages between people. Repeating lamps, theatrical grounds, limited props, and a consistent UI card material bind orange, teal, green, amber and purple into one world. Do not infer exact focal lengths or production methods from these pixels, and do not imply this staged narrative proves all product claims without separate evidence.

- f415–477 / 13.83–15.90 s: the view approaches one row, with a small amount/action control at right. The control cycles pale/darker emphasis while the row remains anchored. A restrained angled translucent light shape sits behind it.
- f478–539 / 15.93–17.97 s: cut to isolated dark-ground filter controls. Time range, market-cap, and network controls enter sequentially as the scene tracks along their horizontal arrangement, then pulls back to show them together.
- f540–639 / 18.00–21.30 s: the control group shrinks and a larger trading/list panel rises into view below it. After a reading hold, a portrait-oriented chart/detail panel arrives in front around f640 / 21.33 s; the landscape table stays behind as context.
- f640–690 / 21.33–23.00 s: the portrait detail settles with a green action at its bottom; the surrounding layout remains quieter. Around f691–744 / 23.03–24.80 s the interface clears to a small violet orb and a customization word that types beside it.

- f930–1029 / 31.00–34.30 s: many green buy/red sell pills populate a dark field; the pills reduce into three paired green/orange bars. Labels arrive after the bars settle, turning an energetic field into a simplified metric display.

- f1102–1163 / 36.73–38.77 s: a macro order form types an amount and highlights the buy action. A small branded disc emerges near the action and becomes the moving transition carrier.
- f1164–1206 / 38.80–40.20 s: the disc travels across a rising chart, accompanied by a small user/avatar marker. Its path has a visible trail; the chart supplies continuity between an action and the next view, without independently proving a financial outcome.
- f1207–1261 / 40.23–42.03 s: lavender returns; an availability statement builds and holds. f1262–1285 / 42.07–42.83 s resolves to the Fomo wordmark.

Introduce filters sequentially, then reveal their wider context. Do not infer that trading-chart motion proves a real return. [Source](https://x.com/remy_godet/status/2115445301725335578) · [atlas](dense-b/2115445301725335578-1/index.html) · [timestamps](dense-b/2115445301725335578-1/frames.csv)

**Context:** The creator identifies a new Bitstack identity presented in motion. This is a whole identity film mixing type, brand applications, rendered objects, and app UI.

**Observed sequence:**

- f0–84 / 0–1.68 s: a giant black word is cropped by yellow frame edges, then rapidly reduces into a small complete statement. Scale first supplies impact, then readability.
- f85–155 / 1.70–3.10 s: large speed-oriented typography rises/warps on white; a tightly cut succession of finance and directional symbols crosses yellow, black, and muted mint grounds.
- f156–214 / 3.12–4.28 s: short lines assemble into a savings proposition, with arrows and a Bitcoin-like glyph participating in the typography.
- f223–328 / 4.46–6.56 s: outlined wordmark construction and vector handles appear at enormous scale; the view tracks across letter geometry on alternating dark/mint fields.
- f329–390 / 6.58–7.80 s: the finished wordmark sits centered on yellow. This is a deliberate breather after construction.
- f391–530 / 7.82–10.60 s: a tiny opening phrase expands into large stacked era/savings copy with globe/arrow forms embedded in the composition.
- f531–616 / 10.62–12.32 s: rapid rounded-rectangle applications show the identity in varied contexts: logo studies, construction, dock/social contexts, apparel, poster, stamp.
- f617–750 / 12.34–15.00 s: applications multiply into an arc/stack around a central symbol statement, sweep away, and converge into a central branded card before typography takes over.
- f751–876 / 15.02–17.52 s: typographic arrangements open around a single rendered coin. [f830](stills-b/2115445301725335578-1-f830.png) shows a nearly black coin separated by a warm grazing edge; white words sit around, partly behind, and to the sides of it.
- f877–1060 / 17.54–21.20 s: coins follow into a coil/spiral, turn into a ring, and meet circular typography. Macro framing reveals warm metallic edges; the image changes from one object to a rhythmic many-object system.
- f1061–1147 / 21.22–22.94 s: three rotating coins sit in a stable horizontal composition between two copy lines.
- f1148–1253 / 22.96–25.06 s: a short three-part action statement uses a yellow rounded highlight behind its active word; a vertical UI action list scrolls to a selected item.
- f1254–1390 / 25.08–27.80 s: a white phone-like screen grows, its balance/chart changes, and branded postcard compositions follow. The UI is a visual demonstration, not independent proof of financial performance.
- f1391–1495 / 27.82–29.90 s: yellow physical payment cards sit at shallow perspective; foreground type appears and retreats, allowing the cards to fill the frame.
- f1496–1610 / 29.92–32.20 s: a black typographic breather expands/warps then shrinks.
- f1611–1768 / 32.22–35.36 s: yellow returns, the symbol and wordmark settle, and the identity holds with small fine print.

**Art, camera, and finish:** A bold but bounded yellow/black/mint/greige vocabulary connects very different media. The bunny-like mark, arrows, and coins act as recurring assets. Frontal graphic work alternates with shallow physical perspective and macro object framing. Rotating coins are visibly 3D-looking, but specific lens/camera rigs and renderer cannot be identified. Sparse grazing highlights communicate material without making the whole frame glossy.

**Transfer:** Develop a brand grammar broad enough to inhabit typography, masks, physical objects, UI, and real applications. Use transformation when the same idea persists and a cut when the semantic chapter changes. The longest calm holds are identity/proof moments; high motion does not mean constant motion. Reserve a real outro reading interval, rather than cutting at the instant the logo resolves.

- f0–54 / 0–0.90 s: a globe with lime continents floats on dark forest green; a white pill invites a spin.

A user action motivates animation; slowing rotation leads to a result and reading interval. Spatial orientation functions as information architecture. Avoid presenting the prototype's repeated exploration as a single linear sales argument.

**Context:** The creator frames the work as a logo becoming a larger system. The clip shows a coherent visual identity across a logo, copy layouts, photography, posters, and patterns. It is a particularly useful bridge between editorial design and high motion.

**Observed sequence:**

- f0–69 / 0–1.15 s: a lime block on forest green extends into vertical stripes, then contracts. f70–156 / 1.17–2.60 s, this geometry supports a stacked wordmark, which holds.
- f157–219 / 2.62–3.65 s: a purple ground and peach mark replace the green palette; the wordmark becomes a horizontal lockup.
- f220–288 / 3.67–4.80 s: the striped bar lengthens between the name's two parts and expands vertically toward a rectangular layout field. [f280](stills-b/2115414518910111794-1-f280.png) shows the wide peach module preserving the narrow stripe rhythm at its left edge.
- f289–389 / 4.82–6.48 s: a yellow/gray composition replaces the purple; a short three-line chapter statement appears inside the expanded panel and holds.
- f390–459 / 6.50–7.65 s: portrait photography enters through stripe-like masking and settles. f460–525 / 7.67–8.75 s replaces it with a second portrait using horizontal movement and a shifted stripe edge, now framed in cyan.
- f526–650 / 8.77–10.83 s: the photograph wipes away; the panel contracts back to a lime brand mark on forest green, then into construction lines. This reverses the earlier logo-to-layout expansion.
- f650–810 / 10.83–13.50 s: the composition shrinks into a vertical poster on an off-white ground, followed by a portrait poster. f811–900 / 13.52–15.00 s holds a yellow portrait/copy composition.
- f901–1050 / 15.02–17.50 s: poster image and copy collapse into a closer panel; successive section layouts present color, photography, and usage in different palette states.
- f1051–1165 / 17.52–19.42 s: the panel reorganizes into graphic copy tiles, then holds a green headline. f1166–1250 / 19.43–20.83 s, a line grid takes over and becomes a navy/cyan repeating pattern.
- f1251–1490 / 20.85–24.83 s: the scene contracts into another poster, combines pattern, portrait and copy, and then cycles grid-module variations in green, purple/peach, and cyan/navy.
- f1491–1615 / 24.85–26.92 s: repeating modules coalesce into a square, then a stripe icon, then a horizontal wordmark.
- f1616–1799 / 26.93–29.98 s: the lockup stays stationary while the color field changes through several established pairs and finally rests on forest green.

**Art and camera:** Nearly everything is frontal graphic composition, masks, translation, scale, and changing layout. It gains momentum without a physically simulated camera. The same stripe spacing is recognizable as a logo primitive, text divider, viewport, photo mask, and pattern. Palette changes happen at designed boundaries; they are not arbitrary continuously cycling gradients.

**Transfer:** Specify a brand's geometric relationships before animation: stripe widths/gaps, frame proportions, type alignments, image crop behavior, and palette pairs. Animate the same module into distinct editorial roles. Keep a resolved reading interval after an expansion. Reproduce this relationship between identity and layout using the new brand's own assets and geometry; copying the reference mark is unnecessary.

A collage should culminate in a clear focal object or statement; the final empty field is earned by the preceding density. Treat this as a short transition technique, not a complete sales narrative. # Motion Studio and Skale

Study date: 6 November 2026. Sources: [Motion Studio](https://motion.so/studio), [Skale portfolio](https://skale.solutions/portfolio). Local source HTML is preserved in `web/`. This report distinguishes films from portfolio preview excerpts. Audio and continuous original-speed playback were not reviewed; no sound-design judgments are claimed.

## Motion Studio: Memorable

Original media was identified in Motion's page HTML and retrieved from its asset host with a normal browser user-agent/referrer. File `media/motion-memorable.mp4`: 3840×2160, 25fps, 1,378 decoded frames, 55.12 seconds. The complete source was indexed; all 115 overview frames (every 12th decoded frame, 0.48s cadence) were visually inspected through sheets `memorable-study/sheets/00000.jpg`–`00005.jpg`. Consecutive native-frame windows [370,445), [950,1025), and [1190,1300) were inspected through all 11 dense sheets. A subsequent complete native-cadence thumbnail pass inspected all 23 sheets in `memorable-native-all/sheets/00000.jpg`–`00022.jpg`, covering f0–1377 at 240px per frame. This supplies every-frame thumbnail coverage; fine detail still relies on selected larger windows, not full-resolution inspection of every frame. Source PTS/index mappings and hash are in each study's CSV/manifest.

### Complete chronological map

Ranges below are approximate overview brackets unless a dense range is named.

| Source seconds | Visual beat and execution | What it serves |
|---|---|---|
| 0–~5 | Historical computing footage, large centered short copy, monochrome/faded imagery, changes in image framing and white/black stage | Establishes a long technological trajectory before the contemporary problem |
| ~5–~7 | Modern device/product footage and familiar assistant interfaces | Bridges history into the present with recognizable interfaces |
| ~7–~10 | Contained human/assistant footage on a light field with caption-like text | Gives the concept a human context; this is footage framing rather than a 3D UI move |
| ~10–~13.5 | Screen, code, terminal, robot and glasses inserts; compact verb-led typography | Escalates the range of things agents can do before introducing the limitation |
| ~13.5–~14.8 | Strong forward-directional blur image with short copy | Marks the argument's pivot with a distinct field and energy |
| ~14.8–~18 | Violet maze/path illustration, repeated maze fragments, small agent-status marks on near-black | Turns repeated work into a visible spatial metaphor |
| ~18–~21.5 | A sparse familiar waiting/status composition, increasingly large time/token figures | Uses an everyday UI signifier to embody cost; displayed figures are claims in this reference, not verified benchmarks for reuse |
| ~21.5–~26.5 | Floating outline windows, compaction progress, then real-world skill/activity images | Contrasts accumulating context with learned experience through changes of visual medium |
| ~26.5–~31 | Abstract/historical technical imagery, model diagrams, brain scan, then return to maze | Reframes the issue toward memory and introduces a coherent metaphor for the product |
| ~31–~38.3 | One maze becomes a pair, then many colored completed maze tiles; copy distributed over the field | Scales the concept from one remembered run to a reusable collection |
| ~38.3–~43.5 | Dark graph interface with thin colored horizontal routes and a highlighted violet path; copy occupies positions along the route | Makes recall tangible: the retained route becomes an operational path |
| ~43.5–~46.5 | Three photographic panels and large outcome metrics | Switches from conceptual mechanism to claimed benefit; the study does not validate the metrics |
| ~46.5–~47.5 | Small luminous human figures followed by a glitch-like exit | Returns to human stakes before the identity resolution |
| ~47.5–~51.6 | Dot field, a simple angular route line, particles converge into the brand symbol, then wordmark | Resolves the earlier path vocabulary into identity |
| ~51.6–~54.7, then final frames | Large symbol/wordmark and small URL hold on black; the last frames retract the wordmark toward the symbol | Provides a sustained identity hold followed by a closing contraction |

### Dense windows

**Maze, f370–444 / 14.80–17.76s.** The background maze stays faint and stationary while a bright path head progressively draws a trace. The head encounters red dead-end states; the revealed trace retains identity while direction changes. At approximately the second sheet's middle the background structure recedes and the bright path simplifies, then the composition expands into many separate path fragments. Small warm status marks appear above the repeated paths as the fragments settle into a grid. Text occupies lateral negative space while the central maze does the explanatory work. This is staged stroke/path revelation plus replication; the images do not establish the original implementation or exact easing.

**Collection→route graph, f950–1024 / 38.00–40.96s.** The dense colored tile field clears, then the next graph appears across a visible replacement boundary. This is not evidence that each maze geometrically morphs into its own line. The new graph is established before the violet route illuminates across it. Its head traverses horizontal sections and diagonal connections while the underlying multicolored network stays subdued. Text enters in separate locations and phases. Proposed transfer: establish system context, isolate a path, let the highlight make the mechanism legible. Keep graph data truthful if it represents real product behavior.

**Route→identity, f1190–1299 / 47.60–51.96s.** A thin angular path writes across a dot field; compact copy changes in spatially separated groups. The path changes hue as the line completes. Around f1240–1264 the line/text disperse into a particle field; a central cluster grows denser and resolves into the gradient symbol. Frames ~1265–1293 hold the symbol with residual particles clearing; the wordmark begins revealing near the end of the window. Continuity is conceptual and material: a repeated route vocabulary becomes the brand mark. Proposed routes include seeded particles and vector line masks; these are hypotheses, not creator-declared tools.

### Transfer to the skill

The strongest lesson is the argument's visual continuity: historical context → contemporary friction → maze metaphor → stored paths → graph recall → outcomes → identity. The film uses a recurring relationship to connect otherwise varied media. High motion is selective; the ending and sparse waiting state gain emphasis through contrast. Copy is often distributed around or along the explanatory image rather than confined to one caption box. The film is not evidence for universal pacing or independently verified performance claims. Its audio arc still needs listening review.

Source: [Gawx Art's YouTube film](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LX_4HSqMX5g), published 19 September 2024, commissioned by YouTube. Its credits distinguish Gawx's direction/shooting/editing/co-writing from YouTube's production/writing/mix/color. Do not attribute every contribution to one person.

## Actual visual observations

All 2,455 consecutive decoded thumbnails were inspected across 39 sheets. These are reading windows, **not exact shot boundaries**:

| Decoded frames, inclusive | Observed construction |
|---|---|
| 0–383 | Warm desk introduction; progressively tighter pen/hand/face coverage makes hesitation visible. |
| 384–703 | Room, scratch details and low running views vary scale; brief light-state changes retain spatial anchors. |
| 704–1023 | Diversions and red-lit frustration precede marks, a book and drawn planning material. |
| 1024–1343 | Rotated body framing, blue/red contrast and returning pen imagery bridge idea to execution. |
| 1344–1599 | Clock, equipment and repeated performer views compress different production duties into one world. |
| 1600–1919 | Record changes, editing timeline, calendar push and reaction inserts make selection/deadline/delivery concrete. |
| 1920–2239 | Writing, wider room and longer face coverage allow a quieter passage before graphic messaging. |
| 2240–2454 | Overlaid type, rounded image masks and a white brand destination simplify the closing composition. |

The opening pen imagery returns with changed context. Amber practicals, cool surroundings and saturated performance passages differentiate states; camera movement is only one source of variation.

## Evidence and limits

[Complete frame viewer](creative-process-all/index.html), [exact frame/PTS CSV](creative-process-all/frames.csv), [coverage record](creative-process-coverage.json). Frame 0 starts at source PTS 0; last decoded PTS is 102.250000 seconds. Media duration may differ slightly from rounded YouTube metadata. The study uses the retrieved 1920×1080, 24fps video-only stream; 160px-wide thumbnails are not source-size finishing inspection.

[Selected labeled source-frame sheet](creative-keyframes/sheet-r03/index.html) provides larger composition views and precise source labels. [Consecutive light-state window](creative-light-window/index.html) covers f414–453 at 480px thumbnail width. All output padding is excluded from coverage. Revision 2 corrected mismatched labels; revision 3 further separates visible single-frame composition from sequence/tempo interpretations after CLI peer review. Earlier revisions remain as historical evidence.

Visual order, composition and changing states were inspected. Original-speed playback, motion smoothness, audio listening, exact lenses/rigs, color transforms, and every-frame native-detail review were not performed. Auto-generated English captions were retrieved; they contain transcription errors and do not establish performance or mix quality. The caption text is retained locally, not redistributed in the skill.

## Proposed software-film experiments

These are our applications, not descriptions of a Gawx software production:

- Give an ordinary task a tangible obstacle and visible resolution. A setup can introduce a repeated object or state; its return should convey a change, rather than merely repeat attractive footage.
- Alternate useful detail with enough context to locate the action. Preserve the same case/data/object through a transition; avoid close-ups that hide what actually changed.
- Plan light, material and palette roles before grading. Compare a static frame with the same action under a camera move. In a software renderer, camera motion and lighting are separate controls; neither repairs unclear product proof.
- Treat a stylistic peak as a passage with an entrance and a quieter destination. Protect stable text/proof intervals in both editorial and high-motion treatments.
- Choose whether the close resolves the established graphic language or uses a deliberate simplification/value break. Measure actual legibility and hold duration in the delivery format; do not copy this film's timing as a preset. The visible YouTube plaque establishes brand presence before the white ending, without establishing how that prop/image was produced.

Owner mapping: director/story establish the obstacle and return; art/UI/camera establish readable states; motion/editor connect them; sound/narrator time and audition the actual cut; color/render/reviewer verify the encoded result. The 39-sheet scan informs those decisions without clearing their production checks.

# ROUTINE: direct consecutive-frame study

[ROUTINE, a film by Gawx](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GoTa5ETmQYw), Gawx 2, published 6 June 2023. The creator describes a personal short based on an earlier school assignment. Working copy: 1440×1080, 102.477367 seconds; 2,457 decoded frames. Source description/equipment credits are metadata, not proof of a specific shot's construction.

All 39 [consecutive sheets](routine-all/index.html), f0–2456, were opened and visually scanned at 160px per frame. [Coverage JSON](routine-review-coverage.json) records exact PTS/frame mapping, hashes and limits. Two [larger labeled mechanism sheets](routine-mechanisms-sheet-r02/index.html), a [32-frame finish window](routine-finish-window/index.html) at 360px, and working-source frames f1260/f1776 at 1440×1080 received additional inspection. This does not establish original-speed timing feel, voice/music/SFX quality, or a native 4K finishing review. No playback or audio listening occurred.

## Observed visual structure

- **f0–319:** watch, date card, waking portrait, stove, overhead food, eye and exercise inserts distinguish mundane actions. Blue rooms carry amber highlights; work views frame bright windows with foreground darkness.
- **f320–447:** work, dinner and bed yield to a sustained blue sleeping composition, contrasting short inserts.
- **f448–559:** room/portrait views change within a central slot while action fragments accumulate around it. The center becomes darker than parts of the periphery. Repetition becomes simultaneous context.
- **f560–1174:** photographs, ID cards, microscopic images, diagrams, animals and personal archives expand the vocabulary. Image shape and black surround change.
- **f1175–1468:** tactile camera controls lead to a sharp foreground camera with its human subject blurred behind it. Phone-library detail then changes image scale and density.
- **f1469–2092:** isolated portrait memories, a face seen through water, timer and swimming material vary intimacy and observational distance.
- **f2093–2456:** repeated desk poses return to ink, pen and handwritten pages. A central credit panel and surrounding fragments form a second cumulative mosaic, echoing the earlier layout while changing its materials.

These are approximate thematic bands, not exact shot boundaries. Images alone do not identify rigs, transforms or grading tools.

## Transfer proposals for software films

1. **Repeat with development.** Establish one routine task, then show the same semantic object in changed contexts. Keep data/state continuity; each repetition should add understanding rather than merely accelerate.
2. **Use a cumulative layout when accumulation is the point.** The center can recede during an intentional overload passage; it need not stay the brightest element. When the film reaches actual product proof, establish a readable destination. A second layout can close the argument with a changed result. Test subject identification rather than assuming a fixed central panel is clear.
3. **Alternate density and intimacy.** Combine quiet composition, precise detail and concentrated montage. Neither editorial nor high-motion direction requires constant movement.
4. **Motivate materials.** Paper, screen, archive, reflected image and physical action can represent different kinds of evidence. A SaaS film must use verified product states and appropriate brand assets rather than borrowing this film's personal memories or footage.
5. **Compose before adding finish.** Separate subject/background values and palette roles in layers. Treat selective focus and texture as attention tools; preserve sharp product proof and type where comprehension requires them.

Build a clean-cut animatic and a labeled before/action/result layout to test these proposals. Sound/narration hypotheses remain pending until the actual soundtrack and performance can be heard. These transfers are production proposals, not claims that Gawx uses a software-film formula.

Use `routine-mechanisms-sheet-r02`, not the first generated mechanism-sheet revision. R02 corrects f2352's caption: the finger has cleared the written background, but the credit panel has not appeared yet. The consecutive window shows the credit panel arriving later. Source indices/PTS were preserved; no film frames were edited.

The later CLI review also corrected the first mosaic description: the center changes between room/portrait views rather than remaining one waking portrait. Burned-in subtitles are visible text evidence, separately from any audio claim; matching a visible number does not verify the underlying personal claim. The whole-timeline scan supplies temporal layout evidence that the selected stills alone cannot establish.

# Daniel Schiffer: observed shot-planning tutorial

Source: [How I Plan Shots & Transitions | B ROLL 101](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3mZuJAWH1Ow), published 13 June 2020. Public video-only research copy: 854×480, 24fps, 14,788 decoded frames, 616.166667 seconds. No cookies/login were used. Metadata and source hash are retained locally.

## What was actually inspected

The complete timeline was **sampled every 24 decoded frames**, producing 617 thumbnails across 25 sheets. Every populated cell in those 25 sheets was visually inspected at 240px width. A second pass inspected **all 168 consecutive frames** in [14280,14448), PTS 595.000000–601.958333 seconds, across seven 320px-wide thumbnail sheets. Some frames overlap the sampled pass: 785 thumbnail viewings cover 778 unique source frames. This is not an every-frame scan of the full tutorial or a native-size finishing review.

[Sampled timeline viewer](daniel-1hz/index.html) · [Dense transition viewer](daniel-dense-blender/index.html) · [Exact coverage and sheet hashes](daniel-visual-coverage.json)

## Direct visual observations

At 89–91s, on-screen guidance inventories ingredients/tools; at 120–122s it assigns actions; at 167–170s it turns them into sequence/shot order. Handwritten object/action lists and the later shot list make that planning visible. Production views repeatedly expose performer coordination, low handheld framing and the large side light, alongside finished/raw inserts and a photographed edit timeline.

The dense window shows a specific spatial handoff: pouring continues as the image drops toward the tabletop (f14280–14308); f14309 switches to the blade close-up. At f14334, the view changes to the held cup and ingredients. From f14350 the dark table edge rises; by f14353 a red blending image appears beneath it while the previous wider scene remains above. By f14355, the close blending texture occupies the view. The edge bridges two distinct scenes rather than demonstrating one uninterrupted camera move.

The ending samples around 605–610s return to a stable glass/ingredient composition. Subsequent black source samples are distinct from the last sheet's unused padding. The visual construction does not establish soundtrack quality, speech content, playback smoothness or an exact software recipe.

## Original software-film transfer proposals

These are this project's proposed applications, not Schiffer's own app-film advice or tested implementations:

1. **Plan entities, actions and sequence separately.** First list truthful product entities and states; then valid actions/results; then select the argument's order. Do not start with a transition inventory and invent product behavior to fit it.
2. **Give the transition an action and a spatial reason.** A camera descent can follow an object becoming active, then let a real compositional edge carry the attention handoff. In software, a panel edge, card boundary or approved graphic plane can serve that function without pretending the app itself has hidden geometry.
3. **Preserve enough shared context.** The transition should connect relevant states. A mask can conceal an edit; it cannot prove that an unrelated result belongs to the same user/task/data. UI designer supplies before/action/result evidence and the persistent identifier.
4. **Use stable coverage as the destination.** A demanding move should lead into readable proof. Compare the same beat with a direct cut and a locked arrival; keep motion only when its comprehension or emotional benefit survives that comparison.
5. **Stage and test both halves together.** Motion designer and cinematographer agree on outgoing velocity, crop, boundary shape and incoming composition before rendering. Editor checks the relationship in the whole cut. The compositor owns edge/blur integration; render engineer owns deterministic frame seeking and export fidelity.

Required experiment: create departure → action → edge crossover → arrival → readable result sheets, plus a consecutive-frame strip around the crossover. Inspect at delivery size, then play at original speed and listen separately. Record which method wins and why. No universal timing, constant camera movement, speed ramp or sound effect is prescribed by this study.

## Evidence limits

The study uses a public 480p derivative, not a camera original. No transcript was retrieved; this pass does not paraphrase spoken instruction. Chapters in metadata are publisher labels: intro 0:00, shot list 0:50, tilt-down 4:10, blending 7:23, recap 8:28. No original-speed playback or audio listening was performed. The extraction manifests retain their generation-time unreviewed fields; the separate coverage file records the actual subsequent viewing.

# The Calculus of Interfaces — reference study

Inspected 2026-11-10 for the user's instruction that the video mathematics should work like [Shu Ding's reference](https://x.com/shuding/status/2115082810738479363).

## Actual source and scope

The post links **[The Calculus of Interfaces](https://calculus-of-interfaces.vercel.app/)**, a Vercel Labs research prototype by Shu Ding. The post describes turning a dashboard component into a mathematical function, inspired by **[Cheng Lou's Handwired](https://github.com/chenglou/handwired)**. It contains one 15-second demonstration video. X's direct web response was 403; a public FxTwitter mirror returned the post text, link and media metadata. The primary linked page and its deployed JavaScript bundle were retrieved directly.

Inspected evidence:

- Primary page text and HTML.
- The deployed bundle's operation-graph builder, exact evaluation, forward-mode derivatives, interval evaluation and panel explanations.
- Eight source-video frames at 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 14 seconds, shown in `sampled-sheet.jpg` with source-frame labels. The video is 1920×1080, 30 fps. This is sampled inspection, not every-frame viewing or original-speed playback.
- Handwired's README at revision `257856e3b221140acb4cc4460626b850c0bd4ff1`.

No live control interaction test was performed. Source inspection establishes the implemented relationships, while the short clip confirms the visual presentation. The deployed page offers no source-repository link for the calculus application itself in the inspected HTML; Handwired is its stated inspiration, not automatically the same implementation. `evidence-manifest.json` pins downloaded files with SHA-256 hashes.

## What the example actually does

Its function maps dashboard properties to geometry: card positions and sizes, layout height, wrapping and related metrics. A fixed list of arithmetic operations represents that layout. Different evaluators operate on the **same graph**, so a displayed sensitivity or constraint has an explicit relationship to the rendered result.

The retrieved bundle begins with an operation builder supporting inputs, constants, affine sums, products, ReLUs and steps. `select(g,a,b)` is represented by `b + g(a-b)`. The exact evaluator computes numerical outputs; the derivative evaluator propagates values and directional derivatives through sums and the product rule; the interval evaluator propagates lower/upper ranges, including all four endpoint products. The step evaluator can substitute a sigmoid with a temperature and scale. This is executable mathematical structure, not an unrelated score attached to the interface.

The implementation is piecewise smooth. A discrete branch has zero derivative away from its threshold, while its discontinuity cannot be treated as an ordinary smooth derivative. The softened evaluator supplies a useful approximation near those thresholds; it is a different evaluation mode and should be labeled as such.

The page's explicit limitations are consequential: its component was written manually in this representation; it does not convert arbitrary React or HTML automatically. Text wrapping uses monospace character counts. Its proof statements assume exact arithmetic rather than accounting for floating-point rounding, and its projects/device/font-scale distributions are illustrative.

## How the exploration is presented

The source defines eleven tabs, each with a mathematical operation and a concrete consequence:

| Tab | Mathematical operation | Visible consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Metrics | Partial derivatives and a two-parameter surface | How much screen area cards cover and which property moves that metric |
| Optimize | Gradient-based search on a softened objective, later sharpened | Suggested layout properties reduce message cutoffs and page height, with an explicit change penalty |
| Prove | Interval bounds and subdivision | Regions where a stated constraint holds, fails throughout, or remains near an undecided boundary |
| Breakpoints | Discontinuity/kink detection | Where adding a column or wrapping text changes the layout rule |
| Resize | Jacobian updates inside a valid region | Geometry updates from local linear structure, with comparison against a full layout |
| Transition | Paths between parameter settings | A route that crosses fewer layout jumps |
| Signal | Fourier/Haar compression and quantization | Approximation errors, ringing and changed layout geometry |
| Direction | Partial derivatives of geometry | Arrows showing how changing one parameter moves every card |
| Motion | Sigmoid-softened steps | A formerly abrupt layout change becomes a continuous animation |
| Average | Integration over an input distribution | Expected page height and a comparison with sampling estimates |
| Imagine | Complex-valued extension of the softened model | A 3D view using real and imaginary components of positions |

The sampled source clip reinforces this relationship: a scalar/function statement at 0 s, a two-variable surface and gradient at 2 s, optimization history at 4 s, a derivative-based resizing display at 6 s, exact versus softened layouts at 8 s, a signal approximation at 10 s and a complex-valued layout at 12 s. Equations accompany their visible effects.

## Interpretation for the MovieMaker mathematics

The user's intended direction is best read as **an inspectable, executable calculus of video composition and motion**. This is an inference from the supplied reference, not a claim that the source solves artistic quality.

Start with a function whose output is something the user can actually see:

`scene = F(time, parameters, viewport, content)`

For a bounded first version, parameters might control entrance duration, anticipation, damping, overshoot, scale, focal position, camera travel, semantic-cue offset and readable hold. The same function should drive the frame preview, trajectory/velocity plot, readable-window visualization and diagnostics. A slider should change both the image and the plotted function, with consistent units and one source of truth.

Useful experiments drawn from the source's method:

1. **Motion and derivatives.** Render a real shot from time-addressed position/scale/opacity. Show position, velocity and acceleration beside it. At a join, distinguish an intentional cut from an unwanted discontinuity. Avoid claiming that lower acceleration or jerk is always artistically better.
2. **Parameter sensitivity.** Show what changes in the actual shot when duration, spring damping, font scale or camera distance changes. A local derivative is valid only within its stated smooth region; clipping, line wrapping, visibility thresholds and cuts create boundaries.
3. **Readability as a constraint.** Draw the interval in which complete text is settled, visible and large enough. Compare it with an explicit, adjustable reading-time assumption. A symbolic bound on metadata alone does not prove pixel contrast, lack of occlusion or actual comprehension.
4. **Speech and music timing.** Map meaningful events to semantic landmarks or selected audio cues with declared intentional offsets. Plot the timing error. Do not force every cut onto a beat or every word into an animation.
5. **Constrained parameter search.** Search for settings that satisfy declared geometry/timing requirements while remaining close to the chosen direction. Show the objective, constraints, changed parameters and before/after result. Label any editorial penalties as chosen heuristics.
6. **Robustness across deliveries.** Sweep aspect ratio, viewport size, copy length or font scale and display failures. Call sampled sweeps tests; reserve proof language for a bound that covers a stated continuous domain under explicit assumptions.

These are different from assigning a made-up scalar to greatness. Taste, story, truth, humor, emotional effect and audience outcomes still need human judgment and observed data. The formal model can make motion and composition explainable and checkable; it cannot turn unmeasured artistic preferences into scientific facts.

## Implementation boundaries to preserve

- Keep exact rendering, smooth approximation and empirical quality judgments visibly distinct.
- Label units, domains and thresholds. A finite-difference sensitivity is an estimate unless an analytic derivative is implemented and verified.
- Do not advertise automated React/video compilation when the model was authored by hand.
- Do not reuse illustrative audience/device weights as measured user data.
- Do not claim rigorous interval verification if floating-point enclosures, supported operations or boundary coverage are incomplete.
- Keep the app's established collection/detail layout. The reference contributes a functional mathematical exploration within that layout, not a requirement to copy the Vercel page's visual identity.

## Saved artifacts

- `post-fxtwitter.json`: mirrored post and actual outbound/media links.

analysisMarkdown:
# Second video: Kaye's editing comparison

Source: [How To Make Insane Video Editing With Opus 5.5 (Claude Motion)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FJZkfjM8WhI), **kaye.creatives**, published **2026-11-07**, duration **15:21**. Metadata retrieved 2026-11-10.

## Access and inspection

- Original watch HTML, player response and metadata saved locally.
- The description links [prompts, breakdown and free skill](https://higgsfield.ai/s/claude-motion-2-kaye-creatives-zJgoqE); it contains no direct GitHub links. The linked article and its two skill files were inspected separately by the companion source-review task.
- YouTube automatic-caption retrieval returned HTTP 429. No repeated caption-endpoint workaround was attempted.
- Public English audio downloaded with yt-dlp, format 251-20; metadata identifies language en-US. `reference-audio.webm` is 921.001 seconds, stereo Opus at 48 kHz.
- A separate 854×480 AV1 video stream was downloaded as `reference-video.mp4`, format 397, 24000/1001 fps, duration 920.961708 s. This is a low-resolution research copy, not a delivery asset or evidence of native-resolution visual quality.
- `overview-sampled-exact.jpg` contains 31 inspected source frames, every 720th decoded frame (~30.03 s). `overview-sampled-manifest.json` records decoded index, source PTS, time base 1/24000, source resolution and cell. FFmpeg showinfo output is preserved in `frame-extraction.log`.
- The unlabeled `frames/sample-*.jpg` files came from an initial fps-filter extraction; they are not the evidence sheet. Only `frames/exact-*.jpg` and the exact manifest are used for observations below.
- The exact overview sheet and individual frames at 360.360 s, 630.630 s and 840.840 s were visually inspected. This is **sampled visual coverage**, not every-frame inspection or original-speed playback/audio listening.
- A complete local ASR pass produced 318 timestamped segments in 250.94 seconds using cached faster-whisper small.en, CPU int8, English, beam 5 and VAD. The model processed the full 921.001-second audio; VAD omitted nonspeech. `transcript-asr.json` and `transcript-asr.txt` preserve the output. This is **ASR, not human-verified transcription**: proper nouns are visibly mistranscribed, and no word-for-word quotation should be taken as verified. The first direct PyAV path failed because the installed PyAV 19 API did not accept `metadata_errors`; FFmpeg decoding to a 16 kHz mono float array avoided that incompatibility. No audio was sent to an external transcription service. The raw ASR final segment ends at 921.12 s, about 0.119 s beyond the measured 921.001 s audio duration; this small ASR timestamp overshoot is preserved in the evidence and must be clamped to actual media duration before edit/caption use. `evidence-manifest.json` records versions, settings, coverage and SHA-256 file hashes.

## Source setup

The description defines two tasks: a vertical talking-head edit with captions, B-roll and motion graphics; and a motion-graphics film made from the voiceover alone. Chapter starts are 2:00 test 1, 8:05 test 2, 12:10 results/pros and cons, 14:20 verdict.

The ASR introduction at 111.44–122.08 s says the creator supplied the same raw vertical clip to a motion-designer friend and to Claude. That is the author's described setup, not an independently audited controlled comparison. The introduction invites viewers to guess which result is human versus AI.

## Directly observed source frames

| Timestamp | Observation | What it establishes |
|---|---|---|
| 240.240 s | A motion-skill slide displays several visual reference thumbnails | References are visibly part of the presented workflow; cannot infer their completeness or how the model used them |
| 270.270 s | The chatbot input includes attached files and a lengthy prompt | A structured input bundle is shown; the low-resolution sample is insufficient to transcribe the full prompt |
| 360.360 s | A close-look slide calls attention to the first five seconds, headline and four seconds on the speaker's face | The creator explicitly evaluates the opening's timing and screen allocation, rather than only whether export succeeded |
| 390.390 s | Two vertical edits labeled A and B appear side by side | A comparison is shown; this frame alone does not establish which edit is preferred or its maker |
| 630.630 s | A very small two-line text block sits inside a large dark frame, with a partially appearing critique title above | An example of weak screen occupancy is visible; a still cannot establish exact pace or the full critique wording |
| 660.660 s | A/B comparison of voiceover-driven motion treatments | The two film modes are compared separately |
| 840.840 s | A creator-authored pros/cons table contrasts the two workflows | Author's case claims, not independently measured benchmarks |

At 840.840 s the table gives Claude 45 minutes, 5 reels,free iteration and fresh AI B-roll; it assigns the designer days, 1 reel,stock hunting, direct manipulation and taste/humor/timing. It lists a $200–500 designer cost. The AI cost cell is still blank at this sample. Do not treat these values as current pricing, general productivity gains, objective artistic rankings, or fair like-for-like cost accounting.

## Provisional implications

1. Evaluate editing operations separately: raw footage→edited speech/B-roll and voiceover→authored motion. A strong result in one does not establish the other.
2. Preserve the speaker's meaning when removing pauses or takes. Speech alignment and text presence do not establish that the edit preserved emphasis, intent or a convincing performance.
3. Evaluate opening composition, focal hierarchy, timing and the usefulness of each B-roll insert. More images or animated words do not by themselves establish comprehension, retention or emotional effect.
4. Compare finished candidates with maker labels hidden where practical, but describe informal pairwise preferences honestly. A creator's two demonstrations are not a statistically reliable causal model.
5. Keep iteration time/cost and artistic quality on separate axes. Record the full cost of selection, prompting, retries, cleanup, rendering and review rather than attributing everything to the final generation call.

These are proposed adaptations for our workflow, not measurements extracted from a validated retention study.

## Timestamped substance from the ASR

The following are paraphrases of the automatic transcript, checked for consistency with the sampled frames and metadata where possible. They describe what this creator says and demonstrates; aesthetic judgments and performance claims remain hers.

| Interval | Source substance | Useful adaptation and limit |
|---|---|---|
| 199–278 s | Inputs are raw footage, intended script, visual references and a motion-skill file, followed by an ordinary-language brief | Keep a compact, explicit input packet. Preserve what is known from footage versus asserted by script; more references are not automatically better than a coherent small selection |
| 290–305 s | References communicate preferred layout, style and energy, rather than requiring frame-for-frame duplication | Translate references into motion/composition relationships and taste constraints; make the actual product story original |
| 315–329 s | The first result is a rough draft and iteration is expected | Plan a complete first pass, then diagnose the weakest consequential beat |
| 335–381 s | The creator likes color/caption handling but critiques a slow opening, small headline and an inert middle section; she adds references for the weak section and regenerates | Revision notes should identify the time range, focal element and intended change. Four seconds of a face is not intrinsically wrong; the critique is contextual |
| 407–413 s | Talking-head result A is the human edit; B is the AI edit | Preserve maker labels as hidden metadata during a preference comparison; do not mix the labels with test 2 |
| 428–455 s | Human advantages described are voice-motivated camera movement and sound rhythm; AI advantages include timed type, transitions and mood-matched generated B-roll | Compare expression and meaning as well as mechanical alignment. Neither effect count nor perfect word synchronization establishes quality |
| 469–481 s | The creator reports about 50 minutes for references/chat/iterations versus about 5.5 hours of the human editor's focused work | Record end-to-end effort explicitly. These are self-reported approximate case values, not controlled costs or a universal speed ratio |
| 541–603 s | The second task uses the same recording but keeps only its audio, adds motion-only references and a different skill | Treat footage editing and voiceover-led visual authorship as separate production modes |
| 620–642 s | The first motion pass aligns text with voice, but central type is too small and visual entrances lag the speech's energy; a targeted reply requests correction | Inspect focal scale at delivery size, visual arrival against phrase meaning, and settled readability. A motion clock can be synchronized yet feel late |
| 644–674 s | The creator says the human receives the same voiceover and brief. In this test A is AI and B is human | The maker mapping is reversed from test 1; preserve distinct experiment IDs |
| 696–740 s | She praises AI camera pushes and text changes, and human bespoke topic transitions and icon detail, then expresses uncertainty about which wins for everyday social content | Use pairwise preference with uncertainty; do not invent an objective winner from this tutorial |
| 795–813 s | She criticizes generic outputs from weak direction and correction friction in the chatbot-only workflow: changing a small placement requires another prompt/file | Preserve editable scene/text parameters and local revision scope. Her UI limitation does not apply to every AI or code-based renderer |
| 816–880 s | She values human taste, humor, emotional timing and details, and concludes that AI can support rather than simply replace editing skill | Keep human evaluation in the model. The concluding 80/20 split is rhetorical, not measured decomposition of quality or labor |

The later summary describes 45 minutes versus days and 5 reels versus 1; this differs from the specific earlier 50-minute/5.5-hour case wording. At 834–857 s she gives indicative freelance prices and loosely describes subscriptions/credits as a few dollars per reel. No invoices, token counts, full revision ledger, matched expertise controls, viewer study, retention curve or conversion measurement was inspected. Do not use these claims to fit cost, retention or quality coefficients.

## What changes in the model

This reference motivates additional **hypotheses**, not fitted weights:

- Condition comparisons on production mode and source packet. A footage editor's preservation of meaning and performance is a separate concern from a voiceover film's visual argument.
- Add a diagnostic for visual arrivals versus declared semantic landmarks, including the intended lead/lag. Evaluate the settled hold separately; hitting a word boundary is not enough.
- Track focal scale and composition at the actual target viewing size, and interpret them against the shot's task rather than maximizing object size.
- Keep direction/reference coherence, expression, clarity and finishing in human review; do not reduce them to raw reference count, cut count or action frequency.
- Keep marginal revision effort, reproducibility and editable control separate from artistic quality. More inexpensive variants help only if selection and revision improve the intended outcome.

Neither this tutorial nor its two examples supplies a scientifically validated mathematical model of high retention. The evidence is useful for defining failure modes, candidate variables and a fairer evaluation protocol.
